claims.statement: LL-37 (ropocamptide) is the sole human cathelicidin-derived antimicrobial peptide, a 37-amino-acid amphipathic peptide (molecular formula C205H340N60O53) secreted by bone marrow cells, circulating leukocytes, and epithelial tissue as part of innate host defense.

claims.statement: LL-37 exhibits antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, immunostimulating and potential antineoplastic activities, including regulation of leukocyte chemotaxis and cytokine production and support of wound-healing processes; nonclinical work also reports pro-apoptotic tumor-suppressive activity via p53 induction in some cancer cell contexts.

context.formulation: LL-37 peptide (topical/injected in nonclinical and early clinical research)

extractedEvidence.quote: it possesses "antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, immunostimulating and potential antineoplastic activities."

reviewFlags: antineoplastic/tumor-suppressive activity described is nonclinical (tumor-injection) evidence and must not be read as a demonstrated human anti-cancer benefit

claims.statement: FDA lists cathelicidin LL-37 among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn from consideration for the 503A compounding bulks list, stating that compounded drugs containing it may pose immunogenicity risk for certain routes of administration and complexities regarding peptide-related impurities and API characterization, that FDA lacks sufficient safety information to know whether the drug would cause harm when administered to humans, and that nonclinical research suggests detrimental effects on male reproduction and protumorigenic potential in some tissues.

claims.statement: In a phase IIb, multicentric, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 149 patients (144 in the full analysis set) with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers, topical LL-37 (0.5 or 1.6 mg/mL, twice weekly) did not significantly improve complete wound closure versus placebo in the overall population (26.5% and 24.7% vs 25.3%, p>0.05); a post-hoc subgroup analysis in larger ulcers (≥10 cm²) found the 0.5 mg/mL dose significantly improved wound closure (28.1% vs 8.1%, p=0.0458) and healing rate versus placebo. The study drug was reported well tolerated, with six serious adverse events judged possibly (none probably) treatment-related and no deaths.

context.population: adults with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers (mean age 67.6 years, median ulcer duration 618 days, mean wound size 11.6 cm²)
context.formulation: topical LL-37 solution, 0.5 mg/mL or 1.6 mg/mL
context.useCase: hard-to-heal venous leg ulcer wound healing (investigational)
context.doseText: 0.5 mg/mL or 1.6 mg/mL applied twice weekly for 13 weeks after a 3-week open-label run-in (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

claims.statement: LL-37 is sold by research-chemical/peptide vendors framed around antimicrobial, wound-healing, and 'innate immune response' research applications, but the only substantive human controlled-trial evidence located is a single topical trial in venous leg ulcers whose overall result was negative; no human evidence was identified supporting systemic immune-support, anti-aging, longevity, or general antimicrobial-supplementation uses for which cathelicidin/LL-37 products are informally marketed, and FDA states it lacks sufficient safety information on the compound in humans.

conflicts.summary: The 2021 phase IIb RCT's primary (overall-population) endpoint for wound closure was statistically negative, while a post-hoc subgroup analysis restricted to larger ulcers showed a statistically significant benefit; these two results within the same trial point in different directions and the subgroup finding has not been confirmed in a dedicated follow-up trial.
